claims.text: Helm is a graduated Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) project.
Helm packages Kubernetes applications as charts, which are directories of templated YAML manifests, a `values.yaml` file of default inputs, and metadata.
The `helm` CLI renders chart templates using Go template syntax and either installs the resulting manifests into a cluster as a release or prints them to stdout.
Helm charts are distributed through Helm repositories and indexed publicly on Artifact Hub.
Helm is open source under the Apache License 2.0.
The Helm project does not ship a commercial tier.
Pulumi supports general-purpose languages (with loops, conditionals, classes, and package management) plus YAML and HCL for authoring infrastructure.
Helm charts are authored as YAML manifests with Go template syntax and a `values.yaml` file for inputs.
Pulumi derives resource ordering from the dependency graph: each resource waits for its dependencies to become ready, and independent resources deploy in parallel.
Helm installs resources in a fixed order by Kubernetes kind, as defined in the Helm source file pkg/release/v1/util/kind_sorter.go.
Helm chart authors can't declare dependencies between resources or subcharts, except through hook weights.
Pulumi's Automation API is a programmatic SDK in every supported Pulumi language for embedding `up`, `preview`, and `destroy` in a host application.
The Helm SDK is available in Go only; other languages must shell out to the `helm` CLI.
Pulumi Policies is open source, with policy rules written in Python, TypeScript, or Open Policy Agent Rego.
Pulumi Cloud adds centralized policy management on top of Pulumi Policies.
The Pulumi Enterprise edition adds Pulumi-maintained policy packs for CIS, PCI DSS, HITRUST, and NIST.
Helm has no native policy engine; policy is typically delegated to Kubernetes admission controllers such as Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper.
Pulumi is open source under the Apache License 2.0.
Helm is open source under the Apache License 2.0.
Helm doesn't let a chart author declare that one resource depends on another.

The Helm docs state that "the Kubernetes objects from the charts and all its dependencies are aggregated into a single set; then sorted by type followed by name; and then created/updated in that order."

Helm's install order is a hardcoded list of Kubernetes kinds in the Helm source (kind_sorter.go), beginning with PriorityClasses and Namespaces, then Secrets and ConfigMaps, then CustomResourceDefinitions and RBAC, then Services and workloads.
In Helm's kind ordering, any Kubernetes kind not on the hardcoded list (including custom resources) is installed last.
Helm uninstall runs the same kind-ordered list in reverse.
Helm sends the sorted manifests to the Kubernetes API server in a single pass and doesn't wait for one resource to become ready before applying the next.
Helm chart dependencies are a packaging mechanism and don't change install ordering: a subchart's objects are merged into the parent chart's set and sorted by kind along with everything else.
A Helm chart can't express "install the database subchart before the application subchart" or "start this Deployment after that Job completes."
Helm's workarounds for ordering are chart hooks ordered with `helm.sh/hook-weight` annotations, or sequencing logic in the application such as init containers that poll for a dependency.
Resources created by Helm chart hooks are not managed by Helm as part of the release.
Native sequencing for resources and subcharts in Helm has been proposed in HIP-0025, which is still a draft.
Pulumi orders operations from the program's actual dependencies; passing one resource's output into another or setting the `dependsOn` resource option creates an edge in the dependency graph.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider waits for each resource to become ready before creating the resources that depend on it.
Pulumi deploys independent resources in parallel, so updates are faster than a strict serial sequence.
Pulumi deletes resources following the same dependency graph in reverse.

The Pulumi Kubernetes provider's `helm.v4.Chart` supports the `config.kubernetes.io/depends-on` annotation for ordering between objects inside the chart, and `dependsOn` on the chart for dependencies on resources outside it.
Helm manages Kubernetes resources only; anything outside the cluster (a managed database, DNS record, IAM role, managed Redis instance) needs another tool.
The Pulumi Registry covers AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, and SaaS platforms like Datadog, Auth0, GitHub, and Cloudflare.
Helm records each install or upgrade as a numbered release revision, and `helm rollback` restores a prior revision.
Pulumi runs through the local CLI, programmatically through the Automation API, or remotely through Pulumi Deployments.
A failed Pulumi update leaves the stack partially updated, and you roll forward by reverting program code and running `pulumi up`.
Helm favors fast revision-based rollback of a single release; Pulumi favors scriptable control over resources from many providers in one update.
Helm and Pulumi are commonly used in combination rather than as substitutes.
Two patterns (orchestrating a production-ready cluster end-to-end, and wiring Pulumi outputs into chart values) cover most production deployments of Pulumi with Helm.

A single Pulumi program can create the cluster (EKS, AKS, or GKE), configure networking and IAM, and install cert-manager, ingress-nginx, and external-dns through `helm.v4.Chart` or `helm.v3.Release`.
The Pulumi EKS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/eks/ walks through the pattern of creating a cluster and installing the operational stack via Helm end-to-end.

Resource outputs from elsewhere in a Pulumi program (such as a database connection string from `aws.rds.Instance`, a KMS key ARN, a managed Redis endpoint, or a Cloudflare zone ID) flow into a Helm chart's `values` input as typed Pulumi outputs.
Pulumi resolves chart values at deploy time and orders the chart install after its dependencies, so charts can consume infrastructure that did not exist when the program started.
The FAQ page contains a section titled "What's the difference between `helm.Chart` and `helm.Release`?" reachable at anchor #whats-the-difference-between-helmchart-and-helmrelease.
Pulumi creates and deletes resources in dependency order, with each resource ready before the ones that depend on it, rather than in a fixed order by kind.

Pulumi's Automation API is an embeddable SDK for driving deployments from a host application such as an internal developer platform, a SaaS product, or ephemeral preview environments per pull request.
There are three common ways to adopt Pulumi alongside or in place of Helm, and they can be combined.
Using Helm charts directly from a Pulumi program with `helm.v4.Chart` or `helm.v3.Release` is the most common adoption pattern for adopting Pulumi alongside Helm.
Rendering a Helm chart with `helm template` and converting the YAML with `pulumi convert --from kubernetes` produces native Pulumi code.
`pulumi import` and the `import` resource option bring already-provisioned in-cluster Kubernetes resources under Pulumi management and generate the corresponding code.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider exposes Helm charts as first-class resources through `helm.v4.Chart` and `helm.v3.Release`.

A Pulumi program can pull charts from any Helm repository (public or private), pass values as typed Pulumi inputs including outputs from other Pulumi resources, and manage chart lifecycle alongside other infrastructure.

`helm.v4.Chart` renders chart templates locally and registers each Kubernetes object the chart produces as an individual Pulumi resource, so every child shows up in plan output, drift detection, and state.
`helm.v3.Release` uses the embedded Helm SDK and creates a real Helm release in the cluster, preserving Helm-specific behaviors like chart hooks, post-rendering, and release history.

Helm chart dependencies cannot control the order resources are installed in: Helm merges the objects from a chart and all its dependencies into a single set, sorts them by Kubernetes kind, and applies them in that order, so declaring a subchart as a dependency doesn't make it install first.
Ordering within a Helm release requires chart hooks with hook weights or logic in the application itself.
The page section "Resource ordering and dependencies" exists at anchor #resource-ordering-and-dependencies.
Teams can keep installing upstream charts from inside a Pulumi program, or move off Helm entirely by converting charts to native Pulumi code.
The Pulumi chart `values` input accepts the same shape as a `values.yaml` file but lets each leaf be a Pulumi output.
Pulumi resolves chart values at deploy time and installs the chart after the resources it depends on.

Existing Helm charts can be installed from a Pulumi program for incremental migration, converted to native Pulumi code with `pulumi convert --from kubernetes`, or in-cluster resources can be imported.
